title: USDA hiring 228 workers for new screwworm fly facility in South Texas, with hiring event Nov. 17–19 in McAllen
excerpt: The U.S. Department of Agriculture has begun hiring for 228 positions at the New World Screwworm Sterile Fly Production Facility at Moore Air Base in Edinburg. Applications are open now on USAJobs.gov, and a hiring event runs Nov. 17–19 in McAllen.
content:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture has begun hiring for 228 positions at the New World Screwworm Sterile Fly Production Facility at Moore Air Base in Edinburg, Texas, the agency announced November 10, 2026, according to the Laredo Morning Times and the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS).

People interested in the jobs can apply online now at USAJobs.gov or attend a hiring event in McAllen, Texas, from November 17 to 19, 2026, from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. each day at the Embassy Suites by Hilton McAllen Convention Center, 800 Convention Center Boulevard. No registration is needed for the event, but candidates should bring a resume, because hiring managers will interview on site, according to USDA.

Most of the openings are skilled trades, craft and labor positions, along with biological sciences and laboratory support roles, according to USDA. There are also openings in administration, technology and occupational safety and health.

“Protecting US livestock and wildlife from New World screwworm is a national security priority, and this new facility will drastically boost the availability of sterile flies,” said Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins in the USDA announcement.

Construction on the Edinburg facility is expected to be finished in April 2027. It will be the first sterile fly production facility of its kind on U.S. soil, and it is expected to produce about 100 million sterile flies a week in 2027, rising to roughly 300 million a week at full capacity, according to USDA.

The flies are the main weapon against the New World screwworm, a flesh-eating parasite whose larvae feed on the living tissue of cattle, wildlife and other warm-blooded animals. Releasing sterile male flies stops the insects from reproducing.

The current U.S. outbreak began in June, after the parasite was found in a calf in Zavala County. Texas has had at least 69 confirmed cases so far this year, with the latest found November 9 in a sheep in Val Verde County, according to federal reports. Cases have also been confirmed in Starr and Zapata counties, as Webb Watch 956 previously reported.

For South Texas ranchers, the Edinburg plant is the closest thing to a permanent line of defense: a U.S.-based supply of sterile flies, built within driving distance of the border counties where the pest keeps showing up.

Sources: USDA APHIS announcement (Nov. 10, 2026); Laredo Morning Times (Nov. 12, 2026); The National Provisioner (Nov. 11, 2026).
